ASSIGNMENTS OF ERROR
ASSIGNMENT OF ERROR I
THE TRIAL COURT DID NOT ERR IN GRANTING SUMMARY JUDGMENT IN FAVOR OF APPELLANTS AS NO GENUINE ISSUES OF MATERIAL FACTS EXISTED ON ANY OF THE FOUR CAUSES OF ACTION STATED IN THE COMPLAINT.
V

ISSUES PRESENTED FOR REVIEW
WHETHER THE TRIAL COURT PROPERLY GRANTED SUMMARY JUDGMENT IN FAVOR OF APPELLANTS AS NO GENUINE ISSUES OF MATERIAL FACTS EXISTED ON ANY OF THE FOUR CAUSES OF ACTIONS STATED IN THE COMPLAINT.
vi

I. STATEMENT OF THE CASE
Plaintiffs Richard Jacobs and John Jacob Jr. commenced this action on May 17, 2004. The named defendants in the Complaint were attorneys William Fadel, William Beyer and the law firm of Wuliger, Fadel and Beyer (improperly named as "Fadel & Beyer"). The Complaint included causes of action for malicious prosecution, intentional infliction of emotional distress, breach of fiduciary duty, and invasion of privacy.
The Defendants filed a joint Motion for Summary Judgment on June 8, 2005. Plaintiffs filed a Brief in Opposition to the Motion for Summary Judgment on July 11, 2005. In an Order dated July 18, 2005, that was journalized on July 25, 2005, the trial court, having determined that no genuine issues of material fact existed and that Defendants were entitled to summary judgment as a matter of law, granted Defendants' Motion for Summary Judgment. Thereafter, this appeal was filed by Plaintiffs-Appellants on August 24, 2005.
II. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Dr. John Jacob died leaving a Will designating four beneficiaries, two of whom were Plaintiffs below and are now prosecuting this appeal. Plaintiff-Appellant Richard Jacob, acting pro se, is a licensed, practicing attorney in Ohio. The other Plaintiff- Appellant is John Jacob, Jr.
Defendant-Appellee William Fadel was appointed Executor of the decedent's estate. Upon the death of Dr. Jacob on July 24, 2003, Fadel ("Attorney Fadel" or "Fadel") began to administer the estate in accordance with the express dictates of the
1

Will. He charged no fees for his services because he was the nephew of the decedent. (Exhibit "A" to Defendants' Motion for Summary Judgment, Affidavit of William Fadel.) Attorney William Beyer ("Attorney Beyer" or "Beyer"), was retained as attorney for the Executor. (Exhibit "B" to Defendants' Motion for Summary Judgment, Affidavit of William Beyer). Attorney Fadel and Attorney Beyer are principals and partners in the Defendant law firm.
The subject Will was admitted to Probate Court on October 15, 2003, at which time no objection was made to Attorney Fadel acting as Executor of the estate. During the course of administering the estate, it became known that there were claims against the estate in the amount of $37,494.48 and administrative costs in the amount of $10,87.59 as of May 1, 2004. (Exhibit "C" to Defendants' MSJ, Complaint for Construction of Decedent's Will filed by William D. Beyer, Esq.) At that time, the estate assets were as follows:
An office building on Lee Road in Shaker Heights, Ohio;
. A private residence in Pepper Pike, Ohio ("Kersdale home");
$6,309.37 in the estate checking account;
. Coins of unknown quantity/value in the safety deposit box of the decedent; and
· Miscellaneous household goods of unknown value.
Id.
Item I of the decedent's Will bequeathed a life estate to Betty Fadel, the decedent's sister, of the Kersdale home. (Exhibit "D" to Defendants' MSJ, Will of Dr. John Jacob.) The alternative bequest to the decedent's four children, including the two Appellants, resulted from the sister's admission to a nursing home. Id.
Item IV of the decedent's Will expressly bestowed upon Attorney Fadel, as Executor:
2

"Full power and authority to sell and convey all or any part of my estate, real, personal or mixed, upon such terms and at such prices as he may deem proper, and without obtaining any order of the court therefore." (Exhibit "D"; Item IV) (emphasis added).
Because the estate costs exceeded the value of the estate property with the exception of the office building and residence, the decision was made to liquidate one or both of these two properties in order to satisfy the estate costs. (See Exhibits "A", and "B" to Defendants' Motion for Summary Judgment). Multiple attempts were made to secure the cooperation of both Appellants in order to have the residence properly appraised, since Appellants were living rent-free in the residence of the decedent. These efforts included informal telephone contact, ordinary mail letters, and certified mail. (Exhibit "E" to Defendants' Motion for Summary Judgment, correspondence from Attorney Fadel to all potential estate beneficiaries, including both Appellants). These letters both expressly and impliedly request any beneficiary, including Appellants, to contact Attorney Fadel and/or Attorney Beyer to discuss disposition of the estate property. It is important to note that these letters were sent more than nine months prior to the filing of the subject eviction actions. Both Appellants have admitted receiving, reading, and acknowledging the content of these letters several months prior to the filing of the eviction actions.
Appellant Richard Jacob testified as follows:
Q: They (Attorneys Fadel and Beyer) wanted the house and they wanted the office building to be sold.
A; To be sold.
Q: And you were aware of that in 2003?
A: Yeah. (Exhibit "F", to Defendants MSJ, Deposition of Richard Jacob, Page 54, lines 15-21.)
Appellant John Jacob, Jr. testified as follows:
3

.
Q: Well, you would agree that the first letter they sent to you requesting you to vacate the premises, or at least indicating that the house might need to be sold was August 25th, 2003? You would agree with that, wouldn't you?
A: Yes. (Exhibit "F" to Defendants' MSJ, Deposition of John Jacob, Jr., Page 86, lines 15-23.)
These efforts met with no reply from the Appellants, but did elicit replies from beneficiaries Eugene Jacob and Robert Jacob. (Exhibit "F" to Defendants' MSJ, correspondence to Attorney Fadel and Beyer from estate beneficiaries Eugene Jacob and Robert Jacob.) Upon receipt of these letters, it became clear to Attorney Fadel that there was no agreement among the beneficiaries for the disposition of the estate properties in question, other than sale and disbursement of the proceeds. All the while, estate costs, including taxes were accumulating rapidly. (See, Exhibits "A" & "B" to Defendants' MSJ, Affidavits of Attorney Fadel and Attorney Beyer). Based on the need to fulfill his fiduciary duty to all four beneficiaries of the estate, Attorney Fadel, together with Attorney Beyer as his attorney, were eventually left with no alternative but to seek eviction of the Appellants from the residence as a sine qua non to the appraisal and sale of the residence. (Exhibits "A" & "B" to Defendants' MSJ). This unfortunate circumstance was due to the complete lack of cooperation from Appellants in assisting with Appellees' efforts to properly administer the estate.
If the eviction of the Kersdale home and Lee Road office building had been accomplished, Attorney Fadel and Attorney Beyer could have properly appraised and then sold the subject properties. After satisfaction of the estate costs, the remaining monies would then have been dispersed equally to the four beneficiaries, including both Appellants. (See, Exhibits "A" & "B" to Defendants' MSJ).
4

In accordance with the above-referenced plan, eviction proceedings against both Appellants were instigated in Shaker Heights Municipal Court. At no time prior to the instigation of these eviction proceedings, did either Attorney Fadel or Attorney Beyer receive any direct communication from either Appellant indicating their intent to cooperate with the appraisal and sale of the residence. At no time did either Appellant challenge the authority of Attorney Fadel, as Executor of the Estate, to appraise and sell the Kersdale home. In short, the eviction actions were "last resort" efforts made in order to realize the express desires of the decedent as to the disposition of his estate property and were undertaken only after numerous and repeated efforts to achieve a consensus among the beneficiaries failed. (Exhibits "A", "B" & "E" to Defendants' MSJ).
No allegation was made in the Complaint below that either Appellant owned, or had any ownership interest in either property in question. On the contrary, Appellants were living rent-free in the residence while estate taxes and other fees continued to mount, to the detriment of the inheritance interests of all beneficiaries. The Complaint did not allege that either Appellant was ever "seized" with respect to either their person or property.
Against this factual background, Appellants alleged causes of action against Appellees for malicious prosecution, breach of fiduciary duty, intentional infliction of emotional distress, and invasion of privacy.
At no time during the pendency of the underlying eviction proceedings did Appellants challenge the jurisdiction of the Shaker Heights Municipal Court to adjudicate the eviction effort. The Complaint herein did not allege any defect in jurisdiction or service regarding the eviction actions in question. After motion practice
5

was completed, including a Motion to Dismiss the Eviction Proceeding, a Magistrate of Shaker Heights Municipal Court dismissed the eviction proceeding, but issued no written opinion as to why.
Appellants did not allege that either Appellee ever occupied, or in any way attempted to occupy, or even enter, either property. Furthermore, the Complaint did not allege that Appellees directed any person or party to occupy, attempt to occupy or attempt to even enter the residence or office building; nor did the Complaint allege that any seizure of either Appellants "person" or "property" ever occurred. Important in this respect is the undisputed fact that neither Appellant ever had any legal interest in either of the properties involved in the eviction actions at any time relevant and that no attorney client relationship existed during the subject time period between Appellees and Appellants.
The claims against Appellees amount to dissatisfaction and annoyance on the part of Appellants with having been inconvenienced by the eviction actions and by having their rent free occupancy of estate property disturbed by the Executor of the Estate. Yet, because Appellants had no property interest in the subject properties, have not alleged any severe or debilitating emotional injury, and cannot establish either the existence or breach of any fiduciary duty owed them by Appellees, summary judgment below was properly granted.
This Court recently decided a very similar case involving the same parties. In re: Estate of Jacob, 2005-Ohio-4998, 8th App. No. 85640, Appellant herein, Richard Jacob, challenged the Probate Court's grant of authority to Attorney Fadel to manage the property of Dr. Jacob's Estate. Id. at 22. This Court concluded that the Probate
6

Court rightfully vested such authority in Fadel, as executor of the Estate, and that Fadel had the authority to require the sale of the Estate's property:
The power to manage real property as described in R.C. 2113.311 plainly goes beyond collection of rents and payment of taxes, and includes, among other things, the power to make repairs, insure the premises, and to prosecute actions for forcible entry and detainer. While the executor has suggested that sale of the premises will be necessary to pay debts of the estate, we cannot agree with appellant that the executor does not seek or require the immediate power to pay operating expenses, repair the premises, insure them, rent them, and if necessary evict the occupants, pending either transfer of the property to the heirs or court authorization to sell the property pursuant to R.C. Chapter 2127. Therefore, we overrule the first assignment of error.
Furthermore, this Court refused Richard Jacob's request to have Fadel removed as executor. Id. at 23.
Thus, this Court has already reviewed and approved Fadel's actions as executor in seeking to cell property, as has the Probate Court. Clearly then, these same actions cannot form the basis of a claim for malicious prosecution, invasion of privacy, intentional infliction of emotional distress, and breach of fiduciary duty.
III. LAW AND ARGUMENT
A. STANDARD FOR SUMMARY JUDGMENT
Rule 56(C) of the Ohio Rules of Civil Procedure sets forth the following standard for entry of summary judgment:
!
Summary judgment shall be rendered forthwith if the pleading, depositions, answers to interrogatories, written admissions, affidavits, transcripts of evidence in the pending case, and written stipulations of fact, if any, timely filed in the action, show that there is no genuine issue as to any material fact and that the moving party is entitled to judgment as a matter of law.
Thus, summary judgment is appropriate where no genuine issue of material fact exists, where, construing the evidence most strongly in favor of the non-moving party,
7

reasonable minds can come to but one conclusion, that being adverse to the non- moving party. Eagle v. Matthews-Click-Bauman, Inc. (1995), 104 Ohio App. 3d 792 citing Bostic v. Connor (1988), 37 Ohio St. 3d 144 and Norris v. Ohio Standard Oil Co. (1982), 70 Ohio St. 2d 1.
The party moving for summary judgment bears the initial burden of demonstrating that there is no genuine issue as to any material fact on the essential elements of a non-moving party's claims. Dresher v. Burt, (1996), 75 Ohio St. 3d 280. However, a non-moving party has a reciprocal burden outlined in Ohio Rule of Civil Procedure 56(E), to set forth specific facts showing that there is a genuine issue for trial. Id. Ohio Rules of Civil Procedure 56(E) states in relevant part:
When a motion for summary judgment is made and supported as provided in this Rule, and adverse party may not rest upon the mere allegations or denials in his pleading, but his response, by affidavit or otherwise provided in this Rule, must set forth specific facts showing that there is a genuine issue for trial. If he does not so respond, summary judgment, if appropriate, shall be entered against him.
B. ASSIGNMENT OF ERROR I
THE TRIAL COURT DID NOT ERR IN GRANTING SUMMARY JUDGMENT IN FAVOR OF APPELLANTS AS NO GENUINE ISSUES OF MATERIAL FACTS EXISTED ON ANY OF THE FOUR CAUSES OF ACTION STATED IN THE COMPLAINT.
1. No Genuine Issues of Material Fact Existed as to the Claims for Malicious Prosecution
Under Ohio law, the elements necessary to establish a prima facie case of malicious prosecution are as follows:
1. Malice in instituting or continuing the prosecution.
2. Lack of probable cause.
3. Termination of prosecution in favor of Defendant.
8

Trussell v. General Motors Corp. (1990), 53 Ohio St.3d 142, syllabus, Davis v. Tunison, (1959) 168 Ohio St. 471, 155 N.E.2d 904.
In order to recover for malicious civil prosecution in Ohio, the plaintiff must prove four essential elements: (1) malicious institution of prior proceedings against the plaintiff by defendant; (2) lack of probable cause for the filing of the prior lawsuit; (3) termination of the prior proceedings in plaintiff's favor; and (4) seizure of plaintiff's person or property during the course of the prior proceedings. See Robb v. Chagrin Lagoons Yacht Club, Inc. (1996), 75 Ohio St.3d 264. In Beechler v. Peterman (Dec. 7, 1999), 9th App. No. 99AP-386, the court stated the following in regard to the seizure element for the tort of civil malicious prosecution:
The Ohio Supreme Court has recently held that seizure of plaintiff's person or property is an essential element to prove a claim for civil malicious prosecution under Ohio law. See Robb, supra. In so doing, the court rejected the arguments raised by Peterman here, holding that "the interests of justice and judicial economy are best served by continuing to require the element of seizure of property in malicious civil prosecution cases." Id. at 270.
In Salem Twshp. Zoning Comm. v. Lynch (Aug. 16, 1999), 12th App No. CA98- 10-133, the Court, also citing Robb, stated:
In reviewing the record, we agree with the trial court that appellant cannot establish a prima facie case of malicious prosecution. Even assuming appellant could show the other three elements were established in the record, a claim of civil malicious prosecution "will lie only in cases where there is a prejudgment seizure of property, i.e., where there essentially has been a judgment against, and a concomitant injury suffered by, a defendant before he has had a chance to defend himself." Robb v. Chagrin Lagoons Yacht Club, Inc. (1996), 75 Ohio St. 3d 264, 270. (emphasis added)
9

In order to successfully assert a malicious prosecution claim, expert testimony is required when it is necessary to establish any one of the elements of the claims. Johnson v. City of Dublin, 2000 WL 726785 (Ohio App. 10th Dist.); also see Jones v. Hawkes Hospital (1964), 175 Ohio St. 503, (setting forth general requirements of expert testimony). In Johnson, the Appellate Court affirmed the Trial Court's granting of summary judgment in favor of defendant when plaintiff failed to support his malicious prosecution claim with expert evidence. Id.
With respect to the element of malice, "[t]he requirement of malice turns directly on the defendant's state of mind. Malice is the state of mind under which a person intentionally does a wrongful act without a reasonable lawful excuse and with the intent to inflict injury or under circumstances from which the law will infer an evil intent. * * * For purposes of malicious prosecution it means an improper purpose, or any purpose other than the legitimate interest of bringing an offender to justice." Criss v. Springfield Twp. (1990), 56 Ohio St.3d 82, 84-85.
2. Appellants Failed to Offer Sufficient Evidence as to any of the Four Elements of Malicious Prosecution.
Here, Appellants have alleged that Appellees filed eviction actions against them in the Shaker Heights Municipal Court "without probable cause." Appellants developed no expert support establishing what the legal requirements are for maintaining an eviction under Ohio law, or when the filing of such an action is legally improper. No specific reference was made in Appellants' Complaint, nor was any evidence proffered by Appellants in their opposition to the Motion for Summary Judgment, as to what act or omission on the parts of the Appellees constituted the "lack of probable cause" alleged in the Complaint. Under Johnson, such a claim
10

requires expert testimony. Consequently, Appellants' failure to establish any, much less sufficient, expert testimony for their malicious prosecution claim was fatal to their claim under Ohio law.
In this case the alleged malicious "prosecution" consisted of the filing of a civil lawsuit in the Shaker Heights Municipal Court. The Appellants filed the lawsuit in their capacity as duly appointed Executor of the estate which had legal title to the property, and as attorney of record for the same estate. As established in the affidavits of Appellees attached to the Motion for Summary Judgment as Exhibits "A" and "B", the actions were necessary because of the financial condition of the estate and the unwillingness of the proposed heirs to the estate to agree on the disposition of this property. Also, at the trial court level, Appellees put forth unrebutted evidence that Appellants were given repeated notice that the property was to be sold and were asked to contact Appellees to discuss a timetable for so doing that would be agreeable to every one involved. It is not disputed that Appellants ignored these letters.
Appellants failed to submit any evidence of malice at the trial court, meaning that they failed to establish that element of malicious prosecution. The evidence submitted by Appellees, including their affidavits and correspondence sent to Appellants, affirmatively demonstrated the absence of malice. Appellants also could not establish the element of lack of probable cause, as Appellees, as Executor and Attorney for the owner of the property in question, had the legal right and obligation to institute the challenged legal proceedings on behalf of the Estate.
Furthermore, Appellants could not establish a "seizure" of their property, as no property was ever "seized" as the result of the eviction action. Additionally, the fact that Appellants never owned the property in question makes it a legal impossibility
11

that they could maintain such a claim. Neither Appellant alleged that he was disrupted from the residence in the Kersdale home or the use of the Lee Road office building. No evidence whatsoever was offered that either Appellant had any property "seized," or was even disrupted in their use of either the Kersdale home or the Lee Road office building. The failure to establish any evidence of an "arrest" of their person or "seizure" of their property, was fatal to the claim for malicious prosecution.
Appellants failed to establish an issue of fact as to any of the elements of malicious prosecution. As this Court is well aware, the failure to establish an issue of fact as to any of these elements is fatal to a claim for malicious prosecution.
Therefore, Appellees were properly granted judgment as a matter of law on the malicious prosecution claim.
3. Summary Judgment was Appropriate on the Claim for Breach of Fiduciary Duty.
Under Ohio law, the elements of a breach of fiduciary claim are as follows:
1. Existence of a fiduciary duty;
2. A breach of that duty; and
3. An injury resulting proximately from the breach alleged.
Hurst v. Enterprise Title Agency, Inc., (2004) 157 Ohio App. 3rd 133. The Hurst Court stated that a breach of fiduciary duty claim is essentially a negligence claim involving a higher standard of care. Id. To establish a breach of duty in a legal malpractice case, expert testimony is required, unless the breach is within the ordinary knowledge of laypeople. McInnis v. Hyatt Legal Clinic, 10 Ohio St. 3rd 112, (1984); also see Langford v. Dean, 1999 Ohio App. Lexis 4668 (8th Dist.) setting forth general requirements of expert testimony where subject matter is outside the general understanding of lay persons.
12

In the within case, Appellants failed to establish any evidence as to what the standard of care is for Attorney Fadel, as well as Attorney Beyer.1 Appellants failed to produce any expert testimony establishing what specific duty or duties were owed by Attorney Fadel and/or Beyer. Moreover, there was no evidence submitted concerning the specific manner in which Attorney Fadel and/or Beyer allegedly breached their fiduciary obligation, other than the reference to the mere fact of an eviction proceeding being filed against them.
4. Appellees were Properly Granted Summary Judgment on the Claim of Intentional Infliction of Emotional Distress.
Under Ohio law, the following elements are necessary to establish a prima facie case of intentional infliction of emotional distress:
1. The actor either intended to cause emotional distress or knew or should have known that actions taken would result in serious emotional distress to the Plaintiff;
2. The actor's conduct was so extreme and outrageous as to go "beyond all possible bounds of decency" and was such that it can be considered as utterly intolerable in a civilized society;"
3. The actor's actions were a proximate cause of Plaintiff's psychic injury; and
4. That the mental anguish suffered by Plaintiff is serious and of a nature that "no reasonable man could be expected to endure it."
Pyle v. Pyle, 11 Ohio App. 3rd 31. Appellants provided no evidentiary materials to the court below that would even arguably be supportive of a cause of action for intentional infliction of emotional distress. There was no reference to any specifics as to how Appellees improperly prosecuted an eviction action under Ohio law. On the contrary, Appellants relied entirely upon the municipal court's dismissal of the action for
1 Under Ohio statute, Attorney Beyer is not the proper subject of a breach of fiduciary duty claim because he is attorney for the Executor in this case, and owes a fiduciary duty to the Executor and not to the beneficiaries directly. See O.R.C. 1339.18, addressed below.
13

reasons that were never stated. Such absurd reasoning would mean that every civil litigant whose civil action is dismissed on legal or technical grounds could be subject to tort liability on the basis of dismissal of their claims.
An entirely separate basis justifying the grant of summary judgment was the complete lack of any evidence of injury in support of Appellants' intentional infliction of emotional distress tort claims. Indeed, when asked whether he received any treatment, counseling, therapy, etc., as a result of his alleged damages as the result of Appellees' conduct, Appellant Richard Jacob stated as follows:
Q. . . . Have you had any medical treatment, psychological treatment, psychiatric treatment, as a result of the injuries you believe you suffered as a result of ... the conduct and omissions of Fadel and Beyer?
A: No.
Q: Do you intend to?
A: No. . . ("Exhibit F" to Defendants' MSJ, Deposition of Richard Jacob, Page 107, lines 13- 22).
Likewise, Appellant John Jacob testified as follows:
Q. Fair enough. Have you received any medical treatment, psychological treatment, psychiatric treatment at all, as a result of anything that you believe Bill Beyer or Bill Fadel did or should have done?
A: Have I gone to a doctor or psychiatric (sic) -- no.
Q: Any treatment at all?
A: Not yet.
Q: Not yet. Do you have - do you intend to?
A: No, I think I am still sane.
Q: Okay. And I just want to restrict this question to any treatment that you either have received or may receive.
A: Medical treatment I've had, but that relates to my foot.
Q: ... Any treatment at all, whether you've been to a doctor, a psychiatrist, a psychologist, a
14

A:
counselor, a therapist or anyone else, anybody who might be mistaken for one of those people, as a result of anything you think Bill Beyer or Bill Fadel did or didn't do in this lawsuit? No. ("Exhibit E" to Defendants' MSJ, Deposition of John Jacob, Page 239, lines 8-13) (emphasis added)
This testimony clearly demonstrates that Appellants experienced no legally recognized mental/emotional damages with respect to their intentional tort claims, as well as the malicious prosecution and breach of fiduciary duty claims.
Emotional distress suffered by a party must be both severe and debilitating to recover damages under an intentional infliction of emotional distress claim. Paugh v. Hanks (1983), 6 Ohio St.3d 72, 78.
The Eighth District Court of Appeals has granted judgment as a matter of law in favor of Defendants where Plaintiffs have asserted a claim of intentional infliction of emotional distress and then failed to submit any evidence from a mental health professional to support allegations of severe emotional distress. Smullen v. Interfact Polygraphs, Inc., (October 3, 1991) 8th App. No. 58722. In Smullen, Plaintiff submitted only her own testimony about being upset and thus was held to have failed to submit sufficient evidence of a psychological injury. Here, neither Appellant has received any treatment nor intends to receive any treatment for his "emotional" injury. Appellants failed to establish any, much less sufficient, evidence of damages from Appellees' alleged conduct. Appellees were therefore entitled to judgment as a matter of law on Appellants' intentional infliction of distress claim, as well as the invasion of privacy claim.
.
15

5. Summary Judgment was Properly Granted on the Claims for Invasion of Privacy.
Under Ohio law an invasion of privacy actions requires the following necessary elements:
1. A wrongful intrusion into one's private activities; and
2. In such a manner as to outrage or cause mental suffering, shame or humiliation to a person of ordinary sensibilities.
Housh v. Peth, 165 Ohio St. 35 (1956). This cause of action is difficult to understand in light of the following language of the Will:
ITEM IV
I nominate and appoint my nephew, William I. Fadel, Executor of this my Last Will and Testament, . . . hereby granting to him as Executor, full power and authority to sell and convey all or any part of my estate, real, personal or mixed, upon such terms and at such prices as he may deem proper, and without obtaining any order of the Court therefore. ... (Exhibit "D," Item IV).
R.C. 2113.311 provides that:
(A) If, within a reasonable time after the appointment of the executor or administrator, no one in authority has taken over the management and rental of any real estate of which the decedent died seized, the executor or administrator, or an heir or devisee may make application to the Probate Court for an order authorizing the executor or administrator to assume such duties:
(5) Prosecute actions for forcible entry and detention of such real estate.
By vesting Attorney Fadel with the power to sell the Kersdale home and the Lee Road office building, the Will itself, as well as the subsequent appointment of Fadel as Executor by the Probate Court, preempted any claim on the part of Appellants that Attorneys Fadel and Beyer were somehow "intruding" into Appellants' "private activities." Appellants were clearly privileged to take any appropriate action regarding
16

the subject properties by the Will itself. Not only were these Appellees entitled to sell the Kersdale home and Lee Road office building, they would have been derelict in their respective duties not to pursue the sales once it became clear that such action was necessary to realize the testator's express desires with respect to the estate assets as well as to stop the accumulation of estate debt which progressively shrunk the beneficiaries prospective inheritance. Thus, there was no "wrongful intrusion" as a matter of law.
Appellants likewise lack evidentiary support for their claim of an emotional injury with respect to their invasion of privacy claim as was set forth above with respect to their intentional infliction of emotional distress claim. Accordingly, Appellees were entitled to judgment as a matter of law as to the claim for invasion of privacy.
6. Appellees Were Entitled To Judgment As A Matter Of Law Because Appellants Failed To Comply With The Express Requirements Of Ohio Statutory Law Prior To Filing Suit.
Under Ohio law, heirs of a decedent lack standing to sue in their own names to assert claims which properly belong to the estate. Firestone v. Galbreath, 747 F. Supp. 1556 (S.D. Ohio 1990). The only exception carved out of this rule pertains to the heirs first having made demand upon the Executor, in this case Attorney Fadel, to bring the action and establishing that the Executor has failed to do so. Id. R.C. 2107.46.
There is no dispute that the subject matter of the Complaint, the Kersdale home · and the Lee Road office building, were estate assets. Since Attorneys Fadel and Beyer are alleged to have engaged in offensive conduct with respect to these estate assets, Appellants were obligated to make written demand upon Attorney Fadel in his capacity as Executor to forestall the eviction actions in question; of which Appellants had
17

several months' advanced notice. R.C. 2107.46 expressly requires that in a situation such as the one presented herein, Appellants would have had to have called upon Attorney Fadel to prevent the filing of these eviction actions. Id. Both Appellants acknowledge that they were aware of the intention of Attorneys Fadel and Beyer to instigate eviction actions against them in Shaker Heights Municipal Court, as early as January, 2004.
Appellants are also estopped from filing the within claims precisely because of their significant advanced notice of the eviction actions. See Great Lakes Coal Mining Co. v. Troll, et al., 1924 WL 2011 (8th Dist.); (holding that where a party having rights2 permits another to deal with the property in a manner inconsistent with such right and makes no objection, he cannot afterwards complain.) Appellants never took any steps to prevent the filing of the eviction action regarding of they had several months advanced notice.
7. Because Appellants Were Incapable Of Establishing An Attorney Client Relationship Between Themselves And Attorney Beyer, And Attorney Beyer Was Statutorily Immune From Suit, Attorney Beyer Was Entitled To Judgment As A Matter Of Law on All Claims.
An attorney is immune from liability to third persons when the alleged liability arises from his conduct as an attorney acting in good faith, and with knowledge of, on behalf of his client. Scholler v. Scholler (1984), 10 Ohio St. 3rd 98. The policy underlying the immunity extended to attorneys acting in this manner is that the "obligation of an attorney is to direct his attention to the needs of the client, and not the needs of a third party." Simon v. Zipperstein (1987), 32 Ohio St. 3rd 74. Appellants did not allege that Attorney Beyer at anytime represented either Appellant in any
2 Assuming arguendo that Plaintiffs had any "rights" with respect to either property.
18

manner. Attorney Beyer is, and has been at all relevant times, counsel for Attorney Fadel and has represented Attorney Fadel with respect to his administration of the estate. Consequently, Attorney Beyer is Attorney Fadel's attorney, and not attorney for either Appellant. This fact alone precludes Appellants from maintaining any action against Attorney Beyer under both Scholler and Simon. Indeed, to subject an attorney to liability to third persons who he does not represent threatens the capacity of attorneys to zealously represent the interests of their client. Such a result is directly contrary to the attorney's ability to fulfill his ethical and fiduciary obligation to his client. R.C. 1339.18 provides that an attorney representing fiduciaries of an estate cannot be liable for legal malpractice to third parties, whether or not those third parties are vested beneficiaries of the estate:
An attorney who performs legal services for a fiduciary, by reason of the attorney performing those legal services for the fiduciary, has no duty or obligation in contract, tort, or otherwise to any third party to whom the fiduciary owes fiduciary obligations ..
In this case, Attorney Beyer represented Attorney Fadel with respect to Attorney Fadel's administration of the estate. Under Ohio law, as set forth above, Attorney Beyer did not represent the beneficiaries, and, thus, did not represent Appellants. Consequently, Attorney Beyer has no liability and therefore cannot be liable to either Appellant with respect to any allegations set forth in their Complaint against Attorney Beyer.3 For all of these reasons, Attorney Beyer was independently entitled to judgment as a matter of law as to all claims against him. Accordingly, summary judgment was properly granted in favor of Attorney Beyer.

IV. CONCLUSION.
As set forth above, Appellants lacked any expert support for their claims. Appellants concededly suffered no legally recognized damages with respect to their claims of emotional/mental pain and suffering. Attorney Beyer was separately entitled to judgment as a matter of law because he did not represent, nor has he ever represented, Appellants. In addition, Attorney Beyer was statutorily immune from suit by these Appellants, further entitling him to judgment as a matter of law on all claims. For all of the foregoing reasons, the trial court's grant of summary judgment should be affirmed.
